I actually found the mushrooms in the first shot in my back yard. They were very low down in the trunk of a dead tree. I got a small step stool to sit on but still bent over to shoot them. And even then, I used my articulated screen to get lower so I would shoot them straight on. 
I wonder if it's insects or small animals that nibble on them. And hope they're not poisonous.

replies.text: I think keeping it flat and frontal was a good call - the barred window, the pipes, the rough stone, all of it just sits there like a diagram of texture. What made you stop for a wall most people walk straight past?

answers.author: leighw.photos
answers.text: I'm always looking for things others would walk right by

replies.text: This one glows - the red and gold leaves hang in that shaft of light like they were placed there, and the bench keeps the whole frame honest. Was the light already cutting across the wall when you walked in, or did you wait for the sun to drop into that exact slot?

How long did you stand there before the flock wrapped around the tower like that? A whole murmuration swirling around that lit pier, hundreds of birds against the dusk while the sea underneath stays dead calm.

answers.author: sarahlouisebphotos
answers.text: This was towards the end 😊

replies.text: The leaf carpet does all the leading here - orange and gold all the way to the trees, and then the path just disappears into white at the end. How thick was that fog when you walked in?
Pure patience, that one - the bird parked on the ball-top gatepost while the fog eats everything behind it, oak branches framing the perch. How long did it sit still before it lifted off?

The 50mm keeps it intimate - her face soft and close, the daisy floating by her hand, and the green sweater doing all the color work against the autumn blur. Was the closed-eyes moment planned, or did you catch it and keep it?
How long did you wait for the two trams to line up like that? The big Coca-Cola tram in the middle, the cropped one at the edge, and the cobbles doing all the leading.

replies.text: The long exposure turns Superior into glass - the rocks and the tide pool hold still while the whole sky goes soft above them. A blue hour that earns the wait.
One still figure in the middle of all that flight - the fog swallows the city behind him and the pigeons do the rest. The kind of frame that only happens once.

The reflection does all the work - those gold tamaracks doubled in still water, and the frost just proves how cold that morning was. How long did you wait for the mist to lift enough to see the far shore?

replies.text: I think getting low on the boardwalk was a good call - the orange leaves pull the eye straight down to that lone walker, and the bare trees frame the whole walk. Did you plan the shot around the leaves, or did the walker just wander into it?

replies.text: The backlight does all the talking - the grasses glow, the water catches it, and the figure just stands inside the light. Beautifully staged.

Shooting straight up between the towers turns the balconies into a honeycomb, and that pale one in the middle just keeps climbing out of the frame. Were you standing in the gap between the blocks when you looked up?

How close did the swan let you get before it noticed the lens? That orange beak against the white neck is doing all the work, and the golden bracken melting behind it turns a portrait into a painting.
